title: Judith

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 1
summaryBullets: It was the twelfth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, who ruled over the Assyrians in the great city of Nineveh. In those days Arphaxad ruled over the Medes in Ecbatana. (1:1).
He built walls around Ecbatana with hewn stones three cubits thick and six cubits long; he made the walls seventy cubits high and fifty cubits wide. (1:2).
At its gates he raised towers one hundred cubits high and sixty cubits wide at the foundations. (1:3).
He made its gates seventy cubits high and forty cubits wide to allow his armies to march out in force and his infantry to form their ranks. (1:4).
Then King Nebuchadnezzar made war against King Arphaxad in the great plain that is on the borders of Ragau. (1:5).

There rallied to him all the people of the hill country and all those who lived along the Euphrates, the Tigris, and the Hydaspes, and, on the plain, Arioch, king of the Elymeans. Thus many nations joined the forces of the Cheleoudites. (1:6).

Then Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, sent messengers to all who lived in Persia and to all who lived in the west, those who lived in Cilicia and Damascus, Lebanon and Antilebanon, and all who lived along the seacoast, (1:7).
and those among the nations of Carmel and Gilead, and Upper Galilee and the great plain of Esdraelon, (1:8).

and all who were in Samaria and its towns, and beyond the Jordan as far as Jerusalem and Bethany and Chelous and Kadesh and the river of Egypt, and Tahpanhes and Raamses and the whole land of Goshen, (1:9).
even beyond Tanis and Memphis, and all who lived in Egypt as far as the borders of Ethiopia. (1:10).

But all who lived in the whole region showed contempt for the summons of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, and refused to join him in the war, for they were not afraid of him but regarded him as only one man. So they sent back his messengers empty-handed and in disgrace. (1:11).

Then Nebuchadnezzar became very angry with this whole region and swore by his throne and kingdom that he would take revenge on the whole territory of Cilicia and Damascus and Syria, that he would kill with his sword also all the inhabitants of the land of Moab, and the people of Ammon, and all Judea, and every one in Egypt, as far as the coasts of the two seas. (1:12).
In the seventeenth year he led his forces against King Arphaxad and defeated him in battle, overthrowing the whole army of Arphaxad and all his cavalry and all his chariots. (1:13).
Thus he took possession of his towns and came to Ecbatana, captured its towers, plundered its markets, and turned its glory into disgrace. (1:14).
He captured Arphaxad in the mountains of Ragau and struck him down with his spears, thus destroying him once and for all. (1:15).
Then he returned to Nineveh, he and all his combined forces, a vast body of troops, and there he and his forces rested and feasted for one hundred twenty days. (1:16).
crossRefs: Genesis 10:11-12: Nineveh founded as a great Assyrian city.
Ezra 6:2: A royal scroll found in the fortress at Ecbatana in Media.
2 Kings 19:36: The Assyrian king returns and settles at Nineveh.
Daniel 1:1: Nebuchadnezzar comes against Jerusalem and besieges it.

translationNotes.note: A forearm measure, elbow to fingertip, about 18 inches or 45 cm. Walls seventy cubits high, as in 1:2, stand roughly 105 feet tall.
The royal city of the Medes, set high in the Zagros mountains of western Iran. Ezra 6:2 calls it Achmeta and names it as the place the Persian archives were kept.
The Assyrian capital on the east bank of the Tigris, in what is now northern Iraq. It is the city Jonah was sent to, and the seat of empire before Babylon.

translationNotes.term: swore by his throne and kingdom
translationNotes.note: An oath is staked on whatever the swearer values most. A king swearing by his throne and kingdom puts his own rule up as the guarantee that he will do what he said.

stories.keyTakeaway: Nebuchadnezzar rules the Assyrians from Nineveh while Arphaxad fortifies Ecbatana with hewn stone walls and towers. The western nations refuse his summons to war, so he swears revenge, defeats and kills Arphaxad at Ragau, plunders Ecbatana, and feasts for one hundred twenty days.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 2
summaryBullets: In the eighteenth year, on the twenty-second day of the first month, there was talk in the palace of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, about carrying out his revenge on the whole region, just as he had said. (2:1).
He summoned all his attendants and all his nobles and set before them his secret plan and recounted fully, with his own lips, all the wickedness of the region. (2:2).
They decided that all who had not obeyed his command should be destroyed. (2:3).
When he had completed his plan, Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, called Holofernes, the chief general of his army, second only to himself, and said to him, (2:4).

“Thus says the Great King, the lord of the whole earth: Leave my presence and take with you men confident in their strength, one hundred twenty thousand foot soldiers and twelve thousand cavalry. (2:5).
March out against all the land to the west, because they disobeyed my orders. (2:6).

Tell them to prepare earth and water, for I am coming against them in my anger and will cover the whole face of the earth with the feet of my troops, to whom I will hand them over to be plundered. (2:7).
Their wounded shall fill their ravines and gullies, and the swelling river shall be filled with their dead. (2:8).
I will lead them away captive to the ends of the whole earth. (2:9).
You shall go and seize all their territory for me in advance. They must yield themselves to you, and you shall hold them for me until the day of their punishment. (2:10).
But to those who resist, show no mercy but hand them over to slaughter and plunder throughout your whole region. (2:11).
For as I live and by the power of my kingdom, what I have spoken I will accomplish by my own hand. (2:12).
And you—take care not to transgress any of your lord’s commands, but carry them out exactly as I have ordered you; do it without delay.” (2:13).
So Holofernes left the presence of his lord and summoned all the commanders, generals, and officers of the Assyrian army. (2:14).
He mustered the picked troops by divisions as his lord had ordered him to do, one hundred twenty thousand of them, together with twelve thousand archers on horseback, (2:15).
and he organized them as a great army is marshaled for a campaign. (2:16).
He took along a vast number of camels and donkeys and mules for transport and innumerable sheep and oxen and goats for food, (2:17).
also ample rations for everyone and a huge amount of gold and silver from the royal palace. (2:18).
Then he set out with his whole army to go ahead of King Nebuchadnezzar and to cover the whole face of the earth to the west with their chariots and cavalry and picked foot soldiers. (2:19).
Along with them went a mixed crowd like a swarm of locusts, like the dust of the earth, a multitude that could not be counted. (2:20).
They marched for three days from Nineveh to the plain of Bectileth and camped opposite Bectileth near the mountain that is to the north of Upper Cilicia. (2:21).
From there Holofernes took his whole army, the infantry, cavalry, and chariots, and went up into the hill country. (2:22).
He ravaged Put and Lud and plundered all the Rassisites and the Ishmaelites on the border of the desert, south of the country of the Chelleans. (2:23).
Then he followed the Euphrates and passed through Mesopotamia and destroyed all the fortified towns along the Wadi Abron, as far as the sea. (2:24).
He also seized the territory of Cilicia and killed everyone who resisted him. Then he came to the southern borders of Japheth, facing Arabia. (2:25).
He surrounded all the Midianites and burned their tents and plundered their sheepfolds. (2:26).

Then he went down into the plain of Damascus during the wheat harvest and burned all their fields and destroyed their flocks and herds and sacked their towns and ravaged their lands and put all their young men to the sword. (2:27).

So fear and dread of him fell upon all the people who lived along the seacoast, at Sidon and Tyre, and those who lived in Sur and Ocina and all who lived in Jamnia. Those who lived in Azotus and Ascalon feared him greatly. (2:28).
crossRefs: Isaiah 36:1-2: An Assyrian king sends his commander with a great army against Judah.
Jeremiah 46:9: Cush, Put, and Lud named as warriors in a great army.
Numbers 31:9-10: The towns and encampments of Midian burned.
Joel 3:4-6: Tyre, Sidon, and the coastal region named together.

translationNotes.note: Commander in chief of the entire army, ranking directly under the king. Below him stood the strategos, a field general, and the chiliarchos, literally a commander of a thousand.

translationNotes.original: Greek: γῆν καὶ ὕδωρ (gen kai hydor)
translationNotes.note: A formal demand for surrender used in the Persian period. Handing over earth and water meant yielding the land itself and everything it produced, with no terms attached.
The stock image for a force beyond counting. Locust swarms darkened the sky and stripped a district bare of food, which is exactly what a marching army did to the country it crossed.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פּוּט (Put) and לוּד (Lud) - Greek: Φουδ (Phoud) and Λουδ (Loud)
translationNotes.note: Two peoples from the table of nations in Genesis 10, named in the prophets as suppliers of hired bowmen and shield bearers. Put is generally placed in North Africa and Lud in Asia Minor.

stories.keyTakeaway: In his eighteenth year Nebuchadnezzar orders revenge on the west and sends Holofernes, his chief general, with 120,000 foot soldiers and 12,000 cavalry. Holofernes marches out of Nineveh, ravages Put, Lud, Cilicia, and Midian, burns the fields of Damascus, and terrifies the seacoast.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 3
summaryBullets: They therefore sent messengers to him to sue for peace in these words: (3:1).
“We, the servants of Nebuchadnezzar, the Great King, lie prostrate before you. Do with us whatever you will. (3:2).
See, our buildings and all our land and all our wheat fields and our flocks and herds and all our encampments lie before you; do with them as you please. (3:3).
Our towns and their inhabitants are also your slaves; come and deal with them as you see fit.” (3:4).
The men came to Holofernes and told him all this. (3:5).
Then he went down to the seacoast with his army and stationed garrisons in the fortified towns and took picked men from them as auxiliaries. (3:6).
These people and all in the countryside welcomed him with garlands and dances and tambourines. (3:7).

Yet he demolished all their shrines and cut down their sacred groves, for he had been commissioned to destroy all the gods of the land, so that all nations should worship Nebuchadnezzar alone and that all their dialects and tribes should call upon him as a god. (3:8).
Then he came toward Esdraelon, near Dothan, facing the great ridge of Judea; (3:9).
he camped between Geba and Scythopolis and remained for a whole month in order to collect all the supplies for his army. (3:10).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 12:2-3: Israel told to tear down shrines and cut down the sacred poles.
Daniel 3:4-6: Every nation ordered to worship what Nebuchadnezzar set up.
Judges 11:34: A returning victor met with tambourines and dancing.
Genesis 37:17: Joseph finds his brothers at Dothan.

translationNotes.note: Wooden cult poles or planted stands of trees at a local shrine. The Greek translators regularly rendered the Hebrew asherah with alsos, meaning grove, which is how the word reached English Bibles.
A hand-held frame drum, skin stretched over a wooden hoop, with no jingles on it. Women played it in processions to welcome an army back from a campaign.
The Greek form of Jezreel. It is the wide plain cutting across northern Israel between Galilee and Samaria, the flat corridor that invading armies used.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית שְׁאָן (Beit Shean) - Greek: Σκυθόπολις (Skythopolis)
translationNotes.note: The Greek name for Beth-shean, the city holding the junction of the Jezreel valley and the Jordan. Readers of the Hebrew scriptures know the same place by its older name.

stories.keyTakeaway: The coastal peoples surrender everything to Holofernes and greet him with garlands, dances, and tambourines. He garrisons their towns, demolishes their shrines, and cuts down their sacred groves so that every nation will worship Nebuchadnezzar alone. Then he camps near Dothan for a month.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 4
summaryBullets: When the Israelites living in Judea heard of everything that Holofernes, the general of Nebuchadnezzar, the king of the Assyrians, had done to the nations and how he had plundered and destroyed all their temples, (4:1).
they were therefore greatly terrified at his approach; they were alarmed both for Jerusalem and for the temple of the Lord their God. (4:2).

For they had only recently returned from exile, and all the people of Judea had just now gathered together, and the sacred vessels and the altar and the temple had been consecrated after their profanation. (4:3).
So they sent word to every district of Samaria, and to Kona, Beth-horon, Belmain, and Jericho, and to Choba and Aesora, and the valley of Salem. (4:4).
They immediately seized all the high hilltops and fortified the villages on them and stored up food in preparation for war, since their fields had recently been harvested. (4:5).
The high priest Joakim, who was in Jerusalem at the time, wrote to the people of Bethulia and Betomesthaim, which faces Esdraelon opposite the plain near Dothan, (4:6).

ordering them to seize the mountain passes, since by them Judea could be invaded, and it would be easy to stop any who tried to enter, for the approach was narrow, wide enough for only two at a time to pass. (4:7).
So the Israelites did as they had been ordered by the high priest Joakim and the council of the whole people of Israel, in session at Jerusalem. (4:8).
And every man of Israel cried out to God with great fervor, and they humbled themselves with much fasting. (4:9).
They and their wives and their children and their cattle and every resident alien and hired laborer and purchased slave—they all put sackcloth around their waists. (4:10).
And all the Israelite men, women, and children living at Jerusalem prostrated themselves before the temple and put ashes on their heads and spread out their sackcloth before the Lord. (4:11).

They even draped the altar with sackcloth and cried out in unison, praying fervently to the God of Israel not to allow their infants to be carried off and their wives to be taken as plunder, and the towns they had inherited to be destroyed, and the sanctuary to be profaned and desecrated to the malicious joy of the nations. (4:12).
The Lord heard their prayers and had regard for their distress, for the people fasted many days throughout Judea and in Jerusalem before the sanctuary of the Lord Almighty. (4:13).

The high priest Joakim and all the priests who stood before the Lord and ministered to the Lord, with sackcloth around their loins, offered the daily burnt offerings, the votive offerings, and freewill offerings of the people. (4:14).
With ashes on their turbans, they cried out to the Lord with all their might to look with favor on the whole house of Israel. (4:15).
crossRefs: 2 Chronicles 20:3-4: Jehoshaphat proclaims a fast when armies march on Judah.
Joel 2:12-17: A summons to fast, weep, and assemble at the sanctuary.
Ezra 6:16-18: The returned exiles dedicate the rebuilt temple.
Jonah 3:5-8: A whole city fasts and puts on sackcloth.
Exodus 29:38-42: The daily burnt offering, morning and evening.

translationNotes.note: Coarse dark cloth woven from goat or camel hair and worn as a strip around the waist against the skin. It was deliberately uncomfortable, marking mourning or an urgent plea. Here it is put on livestock and draped over the altar as well.
Cold ash from the hearth, poured over the head or sat in. It is a public gesture of grief and self-abasement, saying visibly that the mourner reckons himself as dust.

translationNotes.term: burnt offerings, votive offerings, and freewill offerings
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עוֹלָה (olah), נֶדֶר (neder), נְדָבָה (nedavah) - Greek: ὁλοκαύτωμα (holokautoma), εὐχή (euche), ἑκούσιον (hekousion)
translationNotes.note: Three distinct classes, not synonyms. The burnt offering was consumed whole on the altar with nothing eaten. A votive offering paid a vow already made. A freewill offering was brought under no obligation at all.

translationNotes.term: resident alien, hired laborer, purchased slave
translationNotes.note: The three ranks of dependent attached to an Israelite household, distinguished in Leviticus 22:10-11 when sorting out who may eat holy food. Naming all three means every person under the roof joined the fast.

stories.keyTakeaway: Word of Holofernes reaches Judea, and the Israelites fear for Jerusalem and for a temple only lately reconsecrated after the exile. They fortify the hilltops, and the high priest Joakim orders Bethulia and Betomesthaim to hold the narrow passes. The people fast in sackcloth and ashes.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 5
summaryBullets: It was reported to Holofernes, the general of the Assyrian army, that the people of Israel had prepared for war and had closed the mountain passes and fortified all the high hilltops and set up barricades in the plains. (5:1).
In great anger he called together all the princes of Moab and the commanders of Ammon and all the governors of the coastland (5:2).

and said to them, “Tell me, you Canaanites, what people is this that lives in the hill country? What towns do they inhabit? How large is their army, and in what does their power and strength consist? Who rules over them as king and leads their army? (5:3).
And why have they alone, of all who live in the west, refused to come out and meet me?” (5:4).

Then Achior, the leader of all the Ammonites, said to him, “May my lord please listen to a report from the mouth of your servant, and I will tell you the truth about this people that lives in the mountain district near you. No falsehood shall come from your servant’s mouth. (5:5).
These people are descended from the Chaldeans. (5:6).
At one time they lived in Mesopotamia because they did not wish to follow the gods of their ancestors who were in Chaldea. (5:7).

Since they had abandoned the ways of their ancestors and worshiped the God of heaven, the God they had come to know, their ancestors drove them out from the presence of their gods. So they fled to Mesopotamia and lived there for a long time. (5:8).
Then their God commanded them to leave the place where they were living and go to the land of Canaan. There they settled and grew very prosperous in gold and silver and very much livestock. (5:9).
When a famine spread over the land of Canaan they went down to Egypt and lived there as long as they had food. There they became so great a multitude that their number could not be counted. (5:10).
So the king of Egypt became hostile to them; he exploited them and forced them to make bricks, reducing them to slaves. (5:11).
They cried out to their God, and he afflicted the whole land of Egypt with incurable plagues. So the Egyptians drove them out of their sight. (5:12).
Then God dried up the Red Sea before them, (5:13).
and he led them by the way of Sinai and Kadesh-barnea. They drove out all the people of the desert (5:14).
and took up residence in the land of the Amorites and by their might destroyed all the inhabitants of Heshbon, and crossing over the Jordan they took possession of all the hill country. (5:15).
They drove out before them the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Shechemites, and all the Gergesites and lived there a long time. (5:16).
“As long as they did not sin against their God they prospered, for the God who hates iniquity is with them. (5:17).

But when they departed from the way he had prescribed for them, they were utterly defeated in many battles and were led away captive to a foreign land. The temple of their God was razed to the ground, and their towns were occupied by their enemies. (5:18).

But now they have returned to their God and have come back from the places where they were scattered and have occupied Jerusalem, where their sanctuary is, and have settled in the hill country, because it was uninhabited. (5:19).
“So now, my master and lord, if there is any oversight in this people and they sin against their God and we find out their offense, then we can go up and defeat them. (5:20).
But if they are not a guilty nation, then let my lord pass them by, for their Lord and God will defend them, and we shall become the laughingstock of the whole world.” (5:21).

When Achior had finished saying these things, all the people standing around the tent began to complain; Holofernes’s officers and all the inhabitants of the seacoast and Moab insisted that he should be cut to pieces. (5:22).
They said, “We are not afraid of the Israelites; they are a people with no strength or power for making war. (5:23).
Therefore let us go ahead, Lord Holofernes, and your vast army will swallow them up.” (5:24).
crossRefs: Joshua 24:2-13: A recital of Israel's history from beyond the River to Canaan.
Genesis 12:1-5: Abram leaves Haran for the land of Canaan.
Exodus 14:21-22: The sea divided and Israel crossing on dry ground.
Deuteronomy 28:15-25: Defeat before enemies follows breaking the covenant.
Numbers 21:21-26: Israel takes Heshbon from Sihon the Amorite.

translationNotes.note: The people of southern Mesopotamia. Genesis 11:28 places Abraham's family at Ur of the Chaldeans, which is the origin Achior is pointing back to.

translationNotes.original: Aramaic: אֱלָהּ שְׁמַיָּא (elah shemayya) - Greek: θεὸς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ (theos tou ouranou)
translationNotes.note: The standard title for the God of Israel in dealings with foreign courts during the Persian period. Ezra 5:11-12 and Daniel 2:18 use it the same way, when speaking to outsiders.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יַם־סוּף (yam suf) - Greek: ἐρυθρὰ θάλασσα (erythra thalassa)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew name means sea of reeds. The Greek translators rendered it red sea, and that reading carried through Latin into English.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַמּוֹן (Ammon) and מוֹאָב (Moav) - Greek: Αμμων (Ammon) and Μωαβ (Moab)
translationNotes.note: Two peoples living east of the Jordan, descended from Lot according to Genesis 19:36-38 and therefore kin to Israel. Achior leads the Ammonites while serving in an Assyrian war council.

stories.keyTakeaway: Told Israel has blocked the passes, Holofernes demands to know who this people is. Achior the Ammonite traces their history from Chaldea to Egypt, the sea, and Canaan, and warns that they cannot be defeated unless they sin against their God. The officers rage and call for him to be cut to pieces.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 6
summaryBullets: When the disturbance made by the people outside the council had died down, Holofernes, the commander of the Assyrian army, said to Achior in the presence of all the foreign contingents: (6:1).

“Who are you, Achior and you mercenaries of Ephraim, to prophesy among us as you have done today and tell us not to make war against the people of Israel because their God will defend them? What god is there except Nebuchadnezzar? He will send his forces and destroy them from the face of the earth. Their God will not save them; (6:2).
we the king’s servants will destroy them as one person. They cannot resist the might of our cavalry. (6:3).

We will overwhelm them; their mountains will be drunk with their blood, and their fields will be full of their dead. Not even their footprints will survive our attack; they will utterly perish. So says King Nebuchadnezzar, lord of the whole earth. For he has spoken; none of his words shall be in vain. (6:4).

“As for you, Achior, you Ammonite mercenary, you have said these words in a moment of perversity; you shall not see my face again from this day until I take revenge on this people that came out of Egypt. (6:5).
Then at my return the sword of my army and the spear of my servants shall pierce your sides, and you shall fall among their wounded. (6:6).
Now my slaves are going to take you back into the hill country and put you in one of the towns beside the passes. (6:7).
You will not die until you perish along with them. (6:8).
If you really hope in your heart that they will not be taken, then do not look downcast! I have spoken, and none of my words shall fail to come true.” (6:9).
Then Holofernes ordered his slaves who waited on him in his tent to seize Achior and take him away to Bethulia and hand him over to the Israelites. (6:10).
So the slaves took him and led him out of the camp into the plain, and from the plain they went up into the hill country and came to the springs below Bethulia. (6:11).
When the men of the town saw them, they seized their weapons and ran out of the town to the top of the hill, and all the slingers kept them from coming up by throwing stones at them. (6:12).
So having taken shelter below the hill, they bound Achior and left him lying at the foot of the hill and returned to their master. (6:13).
Then the Israelites came down from their town and found him; they untied him and brought him into Bethulia and placed him before the magistrates of their town, (6:14).
who in those days were Uzziah son of Micah, of the tribe of Simeon, and Chabris son of Gothoniel, and Charmis son of Melchiel. (6:15).

They called together all the elders of the town, and all their young men and women ran to the assembly. They set Achior in the midst of all their people, and Uzziah questioned him about what had happened. (6:16).

He answered and told them what had taken place at the council of Holofernes, and all that he had said in the presence of the Assyrian leaders, and all that Holofernes had boasted he would do against the house of Israel. (6:17).
Then the people fell down and worshiped God and cried out: (6:18).
“O Lord God of heaven, see their arrogance, and have pity on our people in their humiliation, and look kindly today on the faces of those who are consecrated to you.” (6:19).
Then they reassured Achior and praised him highly. (6:20).
Uzziah took him from the assembly to his own house and gave a banquet for the elders, and all that night they called on the God of Israel for help. (6:21).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 18:33-35: The Assyrian officer claims no nation's god has delivered it.
Daniel 3:15: The king demands to know what god can deliver from his hand.
Isaiah 37:16-20: Hezekiah prays against Assyrian boasting.
Judges 20:16: Slingers who can hit a hair and not miss.

translationNotes.note: Soldiers who whirled a leather pouch on two cords and released a stone at speed. Slings were cheap and accurate at range, so defenders on high ground used them to keep attackers from climbing.
A town was governed by a council of family heads rather than a single official. The text names three of them with their fathers' names, since that is how authority was identified and recorded.
A soldier who fights for wages rather than for his own people. Holofernes uses the word as an insult, demoting Achior from Ammonite leader to hireling of Ephraim.
To speak on behalf of a god, not primarily to predict the future. Holofernes uses it with contempt, since in his account only Nebuchadnezzar is a god anyone could speak for.

stories.keyTakeaway: Holofernes throws Achior's warning back at him, asks what god there is except Nebuchadnezzar, and has him bound and left below Bethulia to die with the Israelites. The men of the town carry Achior in to Uzziah and the elders, hear his report of the Assyrian council, and call on God all night.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 7
summaryBullets: The next day Holofernes ordered his whole army and all the allies who had joined him to break camp and move against Bethulia and seize the passes up into the hill country and make war on the Israelites. (7:1).

So all their warriors marched off that day; their fighting forces numbered one hundred seventy thousand infantry and twelve thousand cavalry, not counting the baggage and the foot soldiers handling it, a very great multitude. (7:2).
They encamped in the valley near Bethulia, beside the spring, and they spread out in breadth over Dothan as far as Balbaim and in length from Bethulia to Cyamon, which faces Esdraelon. (7:3).

When the Israelites saw their vast numbers, they were greatly terrified and said to one another, “They will now strip clean the whole land; neither the high mountains nor the valleys nor the hills will bear their weight.” (7:4).
Yet they all seized their weapons, and when they had kindled fires on their towers, they remained on guard all that night. (7:5).
On the second day Holofernes led out all his cavalry in full view of the Israelites in Bethulia. (7:6).
He reconnoitered the approaches to their town and visited the springs that supplied their water; he seized them and set guards of soldiers over them and then returned to his army. (7:7).
Then all the chieftains of the Edomites and all the leaders of the Moabites and the commanders of the coastland came to him and said, (7:8).
“Listen to what we have to say, my lord, and your army will suffer no losses. (7:9).
This people, the Israelites, do not rely on their spears but on the height of the mountains where they live, for it is not easy to reach the tops of their mountains. (7:10).
Therefore, my lord, do not fight against them in regular formation, and not a man of your army will fall. (7:11).
Remain in your camp, and keep all the men in your forces with you; let your servants take possession of the spring of water that flows from the foot of the mountain, (7:12).

for this is where all the people of Bethulia get their water. So thirst will destroy them, and they will surrender their town. Meanwhile, we and our people will go up to the tops of the nearby mountains and camp there to keep watch to see that no one gets out of the town. (7:13).
They and their wives and children will waste away with famine, and before the sword reaches them they will be strewn about in the streets where they live. (7:14).
Thus you will pay them back with evil because they rebelled and did not receive you peaceably.” (7:15).
These words pleased Holofernes and all his attendants, and he gave orders to do as they had said. (7:16).
So the army of the Ammonites moved forward, together with five thousand Assyrians, and they encamped in the valley and seized the water supply and the springs of the Israelites. (7:17).

And the Edomites and Ammonites went up and encamped in the hill country opposite Dothan, and they sent some of their men toward the south and the east, toward Egrebeh, which is near Chusi beside the Wadi Mochmur. The rest of the Assyrian army encamped in the plain and covered the whole face of the land. Their tents and supply trains spread out in great number, and they formed a vast multitude. (7:18).
The Israelites then cried out to the Lord their God, for their courage failed, because all their enemies had surrounded them, and there was no way of escape from them. (7:19).
The whole Assyrian army, their infantry, chariots, and cavalry, surrounded them for thirty-four days, until all the water containers of every inhabitant of Bethulia were empty; (7:20).
their cisterns were going dry, and on no day did they have enough water to drink, for their drinking water was rationed. (7:21).
Their children were listless, and the women and young men fainted from thirst and were collapsing in the streets of the town and in the gateways; they no longer had any strength. (7:22).
Then all the people, the young men, the women, and the children, gathered around Uzziah and the rulers of the town and cried out with a loud voice and said before all the elders, (7:23).
“Let God judge between you and us! You have done us a great injury in not making peace with the Assyrians. (7:24).
For now we have no one to help us; God has sold us into their hands to be strewn before them in thirst and exhaustion. (7:25).
Now summon them and surrender the whole town as plunder to the army of Holofernes and to all his forces. (7:26).

For it would be better for us to be captured by them. We shall indeed become slaves, but our lives will be spared, and we shall not witness our little ones dying before our eyes and our wives and children drawing their last breath. (7:27).

We call to witness against you heaven and earth and our God, the Lord of our ancestors, who punishes us for our sins and the sins of our ancestors; do today the things that we have described!” (7:28).
Then great and general lamentation arose throughout the assembly, and they cried out to the Lord God with a loud voice. (7:29).

But Uzziah said to them, “Courage, my brothers and sisters! Let us hold out for five days more; by that time the Lord our God will turn his mercy to us again, for he will not forsake us utterly. (7:30).
But if these days pass by and no help comes for us, I will do as you say.” (7:31).
Then he dismissed the people to their various posts, and they went up on the walls and towers of their town. The women and children he sent home. In the town they were in great misery. (7:32).
crossRefs: 2 Chronicles 32:2-4: Hezekiah stops the springs so the Assyrians find no water.
Exodus 17:1-3: The people quarrel with Moses and demand water.
Numbers 20:2-5: The assembly gathers against Moses for lack of water.
2 Kings 6:24-29: A siege starves a city until the people turn on their king.
Ezekiel 4:11: Water measured out in fixed portions under siege.

translationNotes.note: Pits cut into bedrock and plastered watertight, filled by winter runoff channeled from roofs and courtyards. Once an enemy held the spring below, a hill town lived on whatever its cisterns already held.
Flowing groundwater, called living water, and almost always outside the walls at the base of the hill. Taking it was the first move of any competent besieger.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בִּמְשׂוּרָה (bimsurah) - Greek: ἐν μέτρῳ (en metro)
translationNotes.note: Literally water given out by measure, in fixed portions. Ezekiel 4:11 acts out the same practice as a sign of siege, drinking a sixth of a hin a day.
A town gate was a roofed complex of chambers and stone benches that served as market, courtroom, and public square. People collapsing in the gateways are collapsing in the middle of civic life.

stories.keyTakeaway: Holofernes brings 170,000 foot soldiers and 12,000 cavalry against Bethulia and, on Edomite and Moabite advice, seizes the spring at the foot of the mountain instead of storming the passes. After thirty-four days the cisterns run dry, the people demand surrender, and Uzziah asks for five more days.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 8
summaryBullets: Now in those days Judith heard about these things: she was the daughter of Merari son of Ox son of Joseph son of Oziel son of Elkiah son of Ananias son of Gideon son of Raphain son of Ahitub son of Elijah son of Hilkiah son of Eliab son of Nathanael son of Salamiel son of Sarasadai son of Israel. (8:1).
Her husband Manasseh, who belonged to her tribe and family, had died during the barley harvest. (8:2).

For as he stood overseeing those who were binding sheaves in the field, he was overcome by the burning heat and took to his bed and died in his town Bethulia. So they buried him with his ancestors in the field between Dothan and Balamon. (8:3).
Judith remained as a widow for three years and four months (8:4).
at home, where she set up a tent for herself on the roof of her house. She put sackcloth around her waist and dressed in widow’s clothing. (8:5).

She fasted all the days of her widowhood except the day before the Sabbath and the Sabbath itself, the day before the new moon and the day of the new moon, and the festivals and days of rejoicing of the house of Israel. (8:6).
She was beautiful in appearance and was very lovely to behold. Her husband Manasseh had left her gold and silver, male and female slaves, livestock, and fields, and she maintained this estate. (8:7).
No one spoke ill of her, for she feared God with great devotion. (8:8).

When Judith heard the harsh words spoken by the people against the ruler because they were faint for lack of water, and when she heard all that Uzziah said to them and how he promised them under oath to surrender the town to the Assyrians after five days, (8:9).
she sent her maid in charge of all she possessed to summon Uzziah and Chabris and Charmis, the elders of her town. (8:10).

They came to her, and she said to them, “Listen to me, rulers of the people of Bethulia! What you have said to the people today is not right; you have even sworn and pronounced this oath between God and you, promising to surrender the town to our enemies unless the Lord turns and helps us within so many days. (8:11).
Who are you to put God to the test today and to set yourselves up in the place of God in human affairs? (8:12).
You are putting the Lord Almighty to the test, but you will never learn anything! (8:13).

You cannot plumb the depths of the human heart or understand the workings of the human mind; how do you expect to search out God, who made all these things, and find out his mind or comprehend his thought? No, my brothers, do not anger the Lord our God. (8:14).
For if he does not choose to help us within these five days, he has power to protect us within any time he pleases or even to destroy us in the presence of our enemies. (8:15).
Do not try to bind the purposes of the Lord our God, for God is not like a human being, to be threatened, or like a mere mortal, to be won over by pleading. (8:16).
Therefore, while we wait for his deliverance, let us call upon him to help us, and he will hear our voice, if it pleases him. (8:17).
“For never in our generation nor in these present days has there been any tribe or family or people or town of ours that worships gods made with hands, as was done in days gone by. (8:18).
That was why our ancestors were handed over to the sword and to pillage, and so they suffered a great catastrophe before our enemies. (8:19).
But we know no other god but him, and so we hope that he will not disdain us or any of our people. (8:20).
For if we are captured, all Judea will fall, and our sanctuary will be plundered, and he will make us pay for its desecration with our blood. (8:21).

The slaughter of our kindred and the captivity of the land and the desolation of our inheritance—all this he will bring on our heads among the nations, wherever we serve as slaves, and we shall be an offense and a disgrace in the eyes of those who acquire us. (8:22).
For our slavery will not bring us into favor, but the Lord our God will turn it to dishonor. (8:23).
“Therefore, my brothers, let us set an example for our kindred, for their lives depend upon us, and the sanctuary—both the temple and the altar—rests upon us. (8:24).
In spite of everything, let us give thanks to the Lord our God, who is putting us to the test as he did our ancestors. (8:25).
Remember what he did with Abraham and how he tested Isaac and what happened to Jacob in Syrian Mesopotamia, while he was tending the sheep of Laban, his mother’s brother. (8:26).
For he has not tried us with fire, as he did them, to search their hearts, nor has he taken vengeance on us, but the Lord scourges those who are close to him in order to admonish them.” (8:27).
Then Uzziah said to her, “All that you have said was spoken out of a true heart, and there is no one who can deny your words. (8:28).
Today is not the first time your wisdom has been shown, but from the beginning of your life all the people have recognized your understanding, for your heart’s disposition is right. (8:29).
But the people were so thirsty that they compelled us to do for them what we have promised and made us take an oath that we cannot break. (8:30).
Now since you are a God-fearing woman, pray for us, so that the Lord may send us rain to fill our cisterns. Then we will no longer feel faint from thirst.” (8:31).
Then Judith said to them, “Listen to me. I am about to do something that will go down through all generations of our people. (8:32).

Stand at the town gate tonight so that I may go out with my maid, and within the days after which you have promised to surrender the town to our enemies, the Lord will deliver Israel by my hand. (8:33).
Only, do not try to find out what I am doing, for I will not tell you until I have finished what I am about to do.” (8:34).
Uzziah and the rulers said to her, “Go in peace, and may the Lord God go before you, to take vengeance on our enemies.” (8:35).
So they returned from the tent and went to their posts. (8:36).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 6:16: Do not put the LORD your God to the test.
Genesis 22:1-12: God tests Abraham with the offering of Isaac.
Genesis 29:15-30: Jacob serves Laban in Mesopotamia for his daughters.
Numbers 30:2: A man who swears an oath must not break his word.
Proverbs 3:11-12: The Lord reproves the one he loves.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בִּגְדֵי אַלְמְנוּת (bigdei almenut) - Greek: ἱμάτια χηρεύσεως (himatia chereuseos)
translationNotes.note: A distinct mourning dress that publicly identified a woman as a widow and kept her out of ordinary social life. Genesis 38:14 and 38:19 turn on Tamar taking hers off and putting them back on.
Roofs were flat and counted as living space, used for sleeping, drying grain, and prayer. A booth pitched up there gave a widow a private room above the household.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ (rosh chodesh) - Greek: νουμηνία (noumenia)
translationNotes.note: The first day of the lunar month, kept as a festival with offerings and trumpet blasts. Judith fasts every day except Sabbaths, new moons, festivals, and the days before them, when fasting was set aside.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קְצִיר שְׂעֹרִים (qetsir seorim) - Greek: θερισμὸς κριθῶν (therismos krithon)
translationNotes.note: The first grain harvest of the year, cut in spring before the wheat. The work ran through the hottest hours in open fields, which is how Manasseh took the sunstroke that killed him.

stories.keyTakeaway: Judith of Bethulia, a wealthy widow who has worn sackcloth and fasted since her husband Manasseh died in the barley harvest, hears of the five-day oath and summons the elders. She rebukes them for putting God to the test, then tells them to open the gate for her and to ask nothing about her plans.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 9
summaryBullets: Then Judith prostrated herself, put ashes on her head, and uncovered the sackcloth she was wearing. At the very time when the evening incense was being offered in the house of God in Jerusalem, Judith cried out to the Lord with a loud voice and said, (9:1).

“O Lord God of my ancestor Simeon, to whom you gave a sword to take revenge on those strangers who had torn off a virgin’s clothing to defile her and exposed her thighs to put her to shame and profaned her womb to disgrace her, for you said, ‘It shall not be done’—yet they did it, (9:2).

so you gave up their rulers to be killed, and their bed, which was ashamed of the deceit they had practiced, was stained with blood, and you struck down slaves along with princes and princes on their thrones. (9:3).

You gave up their wives for plunder and their daughters to captivity and all their spoils to be divided among your beloved children who burned with zeal for you and abhorred the pollution of their blood and called on you for help. O God, my God, hear me also, a widow. (9:4).
“For you have done these things and those that went before and those that followed. You have designed the things that are now and those that are to come. What you had in mind has happened; (9:5).
the things you decided on presented themselves and said, ‘Here we are!’ For all your ways are prepared in advance, and your judgment is with foreknowledge. (9:6).

“Here now are the Assyrians, a greatly increased force, priding themselves in their horses and riders, boasting in the strength of their foot soldiers, and trusting in shield and spear, in bow and sling. They do not know that you are the Lord who crushes wars; the Lord is your name. (9:7).

Break their strength by your might, and bring down their power in your anger, for they intend to profane your sanctuary and to pollute the tabernacle where your glorious name resides and to break off the horns of your altar with the sword. (9:8).
Look at their pride, and send your wrath upon their heads. Give to me, a widow, the strong hand to do what I plan. (9:9).
By the deceit of my lips strike down the slave with the prince and the prince with his attendant; crush their arrogance by the hand of a woman. (9:10).

“For your strength does not depend on numbers nor your might on the powerful. But you are the God of the lowly, helper of the oppressed, upholder of the weak, protector of the forsaken, savior of those without hope. (9:11).
Please, please, God of my father, God of the heritage of Israel, Lord of heaven and earth, Creator of the waters, King of all your creation, hear my prayer! (9:12).

Make my deceitful words bring wound and bruise on those who have planned cruel things against your covenant and against your sacred house and against Mount Zion and against the house your children possess. (9:13).
Let your whole nation and every tribe know and understand that you are God, the God of all power and might, and that there is no other who protects the people of Israel but you alone!” (9:14).
crossRefs: Genesis 34:25-29: Simeon and Levi avenge the defiling of Dinah.
Exodus 30:7-8: Incense burned on the golden altar morning and evening.
Psalm 20:7: Some trust in chariots and horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD.
Psalm 146:5-9: God upholds the widow, the stranger, and the oppressed.
Exodus 15:3: The LORD is a warrior, the LORD is his name.

translationNotes.note: Incense burned on the golden altar at dawn and at dusk, as commanded in Exodus 30:7-8. Those two burnings fixed set hours of prayer that Jews kept even far from the temple, which is why the text notes the timing.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קַרְנוֹת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ (qarnot hamizbeach) - Greek: κέρατα τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου (kerata tou thysiasteriou)
translationNotes.note: Four projections at the corners of the altar, smeared with blood during the offering rites. A man in danger could seize them and claim sanctuary, so breaking them off strips the altar of that function.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְהוָה אִישׁ מִלְחָמָה (YHWH ish milchamah) - Greek: κύριος συντρίβων πολέμους (kyrios syntribon polemous)
translationNotes.note: Exodus 15:3 in Hebrew reads the LORD is a man of war. The Greek translators rendered it the Lord who crushes wars, and Judith's prayer uses that Greek wording.
The genealogy in 8:1 runs back through Salamiel son of Sarasadai, the Greek forms of Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai, whom Numbers 1:6 names as chief of the tribe of Simeon.

stories.keyTakeaway: At the hour of the evening incense in Jerusalem, Judith lies prostrate with ashes on her head and prays. She recalls the sword God gave Simeon against those who defiled Dinah, names the Assyrian trust in horse and spear, and asks the God of the lowly to crush their arrogance by the hand of a woman.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 10
summaryBullets: When Judith had stopped crying out to the God of Israel and had ended all these words, (10:1).
she rose from where she lay prostrate. She called her maid and went down into the house where she lived on Sabbaths and on her festal days. (10:2).

She removed the sackcloth she had been wearing, took off her widow’s garments, bathed her body with water, and anointed herself with precious ointment. She combed her hair, put on a tiara, and dressed herself in the festive attire that she used to wear while her husband Manasseh was living. (10:3).

She put sandals on her feet and put on her anklets, bracelets, rings, earrings, and all her other jewelry. Thus she made herself very beautiful, to entice the eyes of all the men who might see her. (10:4).
She gave her maid a skin of wine and a flask of oil and filled a bag with roasted grain, dried fig cakes, and fine bread; then she wrapped up all her dishes and gave them to her to carry. (10:5).
Then they went out to the town gate of Bethulia and found Uzziah standing there with the elders of the town, Chabris and Charmis. (10:6).
When they saw her transformed in appearance and dressed differently, they were very greatly astounded at her beauty and said to her, (10:7).
“May the God of our ancestors grant you favor and fulfill your plans, so that the people of Israel may glory and Jerusalem may be exalted.” She bowed down to God. (10:8).

Then she said to them, “Order the gate of the town to be opened for me so that I may go out and accomplish the things you have just said to me.” So they ordered the young men to open the gate for her, as she requested. (10:9).

When they had done this, Judith went out, accompanied by her maid. The men of the town watched her until she had gone down the mountain and passed through the valley, where they lost sight of her. (10:10).
As the women were going straight on through the valley, an Assyrian patrol met her (10:11).

and took her into custody. They asked her, “To what people do you belong, and where are you coming from, and where are you going?” She replied, “I am a daughter of the Hebrews, but I am fleeing from them, for they are about to be handed over to you to be devoured. (10:12).

I am on my way to see Holofernes the commander of your army, to give him a true report; I will show him a way by which he can go and capture all the hill country without losing one of his men, captured or slain.” (10:13).
When the men heard her words and observed her face—she was in their eyes marvelously beautiful—they said to her, (10:14).
“You have saved your life by hurrying down to see our lord. Go at once to his tent; some of us will escort you and hand you over to him. (10:15).
When you stand before him, have no fear in your heart, but tell him what you have just said, and he will treat you well.” (10:16).
They chose from their number a hundred men to accompany her and her maid, and they brought them to the tent of Holofernes. (10:17).

There was great excitement in the whole camp, for her arrival was reported from tent to tent. They came and gathered around her as she stood outside the tent of Holofernes, waiting until they told him about her. (10:18).

They marveled at her beauty and admired the Israelites, judging them by her. They said to one another, “Who can despise these people, who have women like this among them? It is not wise to leave one of their men alive, for if we let them go they will be able to beguile the whole world!” (10:19).
Then the guards of Holofernes and all his attendants came out and led her into the tent. (10:20).
Holofernes was resting on his bed under a canopy that was woven with purple, gold, emeralds, and other precious stones. (10:21).
When they told him of her, he came to the front of the tent, with silver lamps carried before him. (10:22).

When Judith came into the presence of Holofernes and his attendants, they all marveled at the beauty of her face. She prostrated herself and did obeisance to him, but his slaves raised her up. (10:23).
crossRefs: Genesis 38:14: Tamar puts off her widow's garments and veils herself.
Ruth 3:3: Wash, anoint yourself, put on your cloak, and go down.
Esther 5:1-2: Esther puts on royal robes and stands before the king.
2 Samuel 12:20: David washes, anoints himself, and changes his clothes.

translationNotes.note: A fine net hung over a bed to keep insects off. The Greek word passed through Latin into English as canopy. The one in 10:21 is a luxury version, woven with purple, gold, and gems.

Perfumed olive oil worked into skin and hair. In a hot, dry climate this was ordinary grooming, so going unanointed was itself a sign of mourning and taking it up again announced that mourning had ended.
A wound cloth headband, not a jeweled crown. The same Greek word covers the priest's turban, so the picture is fabric wrapped around the head as festive dress.

Dropping face down to the ground before a superior. It was standard court protocol across the Near East, so the same word covers greeting a general and worshiping God, and only context tells which is meant.

stories.keyTakeaway: Judith strips off her sackcloth and widow's clothing, bathes, anoints herself, and dresses in festive attire and jewelry. She leaves Bethulia with her maid and her own food, tells the Assyrian patrol that seizes her she can show Holofernes a way to take the hill country, and is escorted to his tent.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 11
summaryBullets: Then Holofernes said to her, “Take courage, woman, and do not be afraid in your heart, for I have never hurt anyone who chose to serve Nebuchadnezzar, king of all the earth. (11:1).
Even now, if your people who live in the hill country had not slighted me, I would never have lifted my spear against them. They have brought this on themselves. (11:2).
But now tell me why you have fled from them and have come over to us. In any event, you have come to safety. Take courage! You will live tonight and ever after. (11:3).
No one will hurt you. Rather, all will treat you well, as they do the servants of my lord King Nebuchadnezzar.” (11:4).
Judith answered him, “Accept the words of your slave, and let your servant speak in your presence. I will say nothing false to my lord this night. (11:5).
If you follow the words of your servant, God will accomplish something through you, and my lord will not fail to achieve his purposes. (11:6).

By the life of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the whole earth, and by the power of him who has sent you to direct every living being! Not only do humans serve him because of you, but also the animals of the field and the cattle and the birds of the air will live because of your power, under Nebuchadnezzar and all his house. (11:7).

For we have heard of your wisdom and skill, and it is reported throughout the whole world that you alone are the best in the whole kingdom, the most informed and the most astounding in military strategy. (11:8).
“Now as for Achior’s speech in your council, we have heard his words, for the people of Bethulia spared him and he told them all he had said to you. (11:9).

Therefore, lord and master, do not disregard what he said, but keep it in your mind, for it is true. Indeed, our people cannot be punished nor can the sword prevail against them unless they sin against their God. (11:10).

“But now, in order that my lord may not be defeated and his purpose frustrated, death will fall upon them, for a sin has overtaken them by which they are about to provoke their God to anger when they do what is wrong. (11:11).

Since their food supply is exhausted and their water has almost given out, they have planned to kill their livestock and have determined to use all that God by his laws has forbidden them to eat. (11:12).

They have decided to consume the first fruits of the grain and the tithes of the wine and oil, which they had consecrated and set aside for the priests who minister in the presence of our God in Jerusalem—things it is not lawful for any of the people even to touch with their hands. (11:13).
Since even the people in Jerusalem have been doing this, they have sent messengers there in order to bring back permission from the council of the elders. (11:14).
When the response reaches them and they act upon it, on that very day they will be handed over to you to be destroyed. (11:15).
“So when I, your slave, learned all this, I fled from them. God has sent me to accomplish with you things that will astonish the whole world wherever people shall hear about them. (11:16).

Your servant is indeed God-fearing and serves the God of heaven night and day. So, my lord, I will remain with you, but every night your servant will go out into the valley and pray to God. He will tell me when they have committed their sins. (11:17).
Then I will come and tell you, so that you may go out with your whole army, and not one of them will be able to withstand you. (11:18).

Then I will lead you through Judea until you come to Jerusalem; there I will set your throne. You will drive them like sheep that have no shepherd, and no dog will so much as growl at you. For this was told me to give me foreknowledge; it was announced to me, and I was sent to tell you.” (11:19).
Her words pleased Holofernes and all his attendants. They marveled at her wisdom and said, (11:20).
“No other woman from one end of the earth to the other looks so beautiful or speaks so wisely!” (11:21).
Then Holofernes said to her, “God has done well to send you ahead of the people, to strengthen our hands and bring destruction on those who have despised my lord. (11:22).

You are not only beautiful in appearance but wise in speech. If you do as you have said, your God shall be my God, and you shall live in the palace of King Nebuchadnezzar and be renowned throughout the whole world.” (11:23).
crossRefs: Leviticus 22:14-16: Holy offerings are not to be eaten by the unauthorized.
Numbers 18:8-13: The firstfruits and tithes assigned to the priests.
1 Samuel 21:4-6: Consecrated bread handed over only under strict conditions.
Exodus 11:7: Not a dog shall growl against any of the Israelites.
1 Kings 22:17: Israel scattered like sheep that have no shepherd.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בִּכּוּרִים (bikkurim) and מַעֲשֵׂר (maaser) - Greek: ἀπαρχή (aparche) and δεκάτη (dekate)
translationNotes.note: The first and best of a harvest, and a tenth of the rest, both handed over to the priests and Levites, who held no farmland of their own. Numbers 18 makes these their entire living.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵי פַרְעֹה (chey Faroh) - Greek: ζῇ Ναβουχοδονοσορ (ze Nabouchodonosor)
translationNotes.note: A fixed oath formula, as X lives. Genesis 42:15 has Joseph swear by the life of Pharaoh. Swearing by a ruler's life staked the speaker's credit on that ruler's power.

translationNotes.term: what God by his laws has forbidden them to eat
translationNotes.note: Leviticus 11 sorts animals into those Israel may eat and those it may not, and blood is barred outright. A besieged town slaughtering its remaining livestock in desperation would cross those lines.

translationNotes.term: no dog will so much as growl at you
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא יֶחֱרַץ־כֶּלֶב לְשֹׁנוֹ (lo yecherats kelev leshono) - Greek: οὐ γρύξει κύων (ou gryxei kyon)
translationNotes.note: A set idiom for total, unopposed quiet. It comes from Exodus 11:7, where not a dog barks at Israel on the night of the exodus.

stories.keyTakeaway: Holofernes promises Judith safety, and she answers with praise of his power and calls Achior's words true. She tells him Bethulia is about to eat consecrated food and the priests' tithes, and that her nightly prayers will tell her when he can march. He and his men marvel at her beauty and speech.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 12
summaryBullets: Then he commanded them to bring her in where his silver dinnerware was kept and ordered them to set a table for her with some of his own delicacies and with some of his own wine to drink. (12:1).
But Judith said, “I cannot partake of them, or it will be an offense, but I will have enough with the things I brought with me.” (12:2).
Holofernes said to her, “If your supply runs out, where can we get you more of the same? For none of your people are here with us.” (12:3).
Judith replied, “As surely as you live, my lord, your servant will not use up the supplies I have with me before the Lord carries out by my hand what he has determined.” (12:4).
Then the attendants of Holofernes brought her into the tent, and she slept until midnight. Toward the morning watch she got up (12:5).
and sent this message to Holofernes: “Let my lord now give orders to allow your servant to go out and pray.” (12:6).
So Holofernes commanded his guards not to hinder her. She remained in the camp three days. She went out each night to the valley of Bethulia and bathed at the spring in the camp. (12:7).
After bathing, she prayed the Lord God of Israel to direct her way for the triumph of his people. (12:8).
Then she returned purified and stayed in the tent until she ate her food toward evening. (12:9).
On the fourth day Holofernes held a banquet for his slaves only and did not invite any of his officers. (12:10).
He said to Bagoas, the eunuch who had charge of his personal affairs, “Go and persuade the Hebrew woman who is in your care to join us and to eat and drink with us. (12:11).
For it would be a disgrace if we let such a woman go without being intimate with her. If we do not seduce her, she will laugh at us.” (12:12).

So Bagoas left the presence of Holofernes and approached her and said, “Let this pretty servant not hesitate to come to my lord to be honored in his presence and to enjoy drinking wine with us and to become today like one of the Assyrian women who serve in the palace of Nebuchadnezzar.” (12:13).
Judith replied, “Who am I to refuse my lord? Whatever pleases him I will do at once, and it will be a joy to me until the day of my death.” (12:14).

So she proceeded to dress herself in all her woman’s finery. Her maid went ahead and spread for her on the ground before Holofernes the lambskins she had received from Bagoas for her daily use in reclining. (12:15).

Then Judith came in and lay down. Holofernes’s heart was ravished with her and his passion was aroused, for he had been waiting for an opportunity to be with her from the day he first saw her. (12:16).
So Holofernes said to her, “Have a drink and be merry with us!” (12:17).
Judith said, “I will gladly drink, my lord, because today is the greatest day in my whole life.” (12:18).
Then she took what her maid had prepared and ate and drank before him. (12:19).
Holofernes was greatly pleased with her and drank a great quantity of wine, much more than he had ever drunk in any one day since he was born. (12:20).
crossRefs: Daniel 1:8-16: Daniel refuses the king's food and wine and keeps his own diet.
Leviticus 11:44-47: The line drawn between clean and unclean food.
Numbers 19:19: Washing with water, and being clean by evening.
Esther 1:10: A king merry with wine gives orders to his eunuchs.

translationNotes.note: A castrated male official who ran a ruler's household and had access to the women's quarters. The title broadened to mean any trusted court officer, which is the post Bagoas holds.

Ritual cleanness is a status, not hygiene. Contact with foreigners and their food put a person outside it, and washing in fresh water followed by waiting until evening restored it, which is the routine described here.
The Greek word means a drinking party rather than a meal. Food was present, but the wine was the occasion, which is why the account keeps count of the wine.

translationNotes.term: she came in and lay down
translationNotes.note: Guests at a formal banquet ate lying on the left side, propped on one elbow, on couches or on rugs and skins spread on the ground. The lambskins her maid spreads out are her place at that table.

stories.keyTakeaway: Judith refuses Holofernes' food and wine and eats only what she brought, going out past the guards each night to bathe at the spring and pray. On the fourth day he sends Bagoas the eunuch to bring her to a private banquet, where she reclines before him and he drinks more than on any day of his life.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 13
summaryBullets: When evening came, his slaves quickly withdrew. Bagoas closed the tent from outside and shut out the attendants from his master’s presence. They went to bed, for they all were weary because the banquet had lasted so long. (13:1).
But Judith was left alone in the tent, with Holofernes stretched out on his bed, for he was dead drunk. (13:2).

Now Judith had told her maid to stand outside the bedchamber and to wait for her to come out, as she did on the other days, for she said she would be going out for her prayers. She had said the same thing to Bagoas. (13:3).

So everyone went out, and no one, either small or great, was left in the bedchamber. Then Judith, standing beside his bed, said in her heart, “O Lord God of all might, look in this hour on the work of my hands for the exaltation of Jerusalem. (13:4).
Now indeed is the time to help your heritage and to carry out my design to destroy the enemies who have risen up against us.” (13:5).
She went up to the bedpost near Holofernes’s head and took down his sword that hung there. (13:6).
She came close to his bed, took hold of the hair of his head, and said, “Give me strength today, O Lord God of Israel!” (13:7).
Then she struck his neck twice with all her might and cut off his head. (13:8).
Next she rolled his body off the bed and pulled down the canopy from the posts. Soon afterward she went out and gave Holofernes’s head to her maid, (13:9).

who placed it in her food bag. Then the two of them went out together, as they were accustomed to do for prayer. They passed through the camp, circled around the valley, went up the mountain to Bethulia, and came to its gates. (13:10).

From a distance Judith called out to the sentries at the gates, “Open, open the gate! God, our God, is with us, still showing his power in Israel and his strength against our enemies, as he has done today!” (13:11).
When the people of her town heard her voice, they hurried down to the town gate and summoned the elders of the town. (13:12).

They all ran together, both small and great, for it seemed unbelievable that she had returned. They opened the gate and welcomed them. Then they lit a fire to give light and gathered around them. (13:13).

Then she said to them with a loud voice, “Praise God, O praise him! Praise God, who has not withdrawn his mercy from the house of Israel but has destroyed our enemies by my hand this very night!” (13:14).

Then she pulled the head out of the bag and showed it to them and said, “See here, the head of Holofernes, the commander of the Assyrian army, and here is the canopy beneath which he lay in his drunken stupor. The Lord has struck him down by the hand of a woman. (13:15).
As the Lord lives, who has protected me in the way I went, I swear that it was my face that seduced him to his destruction and that he committed no sin with me, to defile and shame me.” (13:16).
All the people were greatly astonished. They bowed down and worshiped God and said with one accord, “Blessed are you, our God, who have this day humiliated the enemies of your people.” (13:17).

Then Uzziah said to her, “O daughter, you are blessed by the Most High God above all other women on earth, and blessed be the Lord God, who created the heavens and the earth, who has guided you to cut off the head of the leader of our enemies. (13:18).
Your hope will never depart from the hearts of those who remember the power of God. (13:19).

May God grant this to be a perpetual honor to you, and may he reward you with blessings because you risked your own life when our people was brought low, and you averted our ruin, walking in the straight path before our God.” And all the people said, “Amen. Amen.” (13:20).
crossRefs: Judges 4:21: Jael drives a tent peg through Sisera's head while he sleeps.
Judges 5:24: Most blessed of women be Jael, the wife of Heber.
1 Samuel 17:51: David cuts off Goliath's head with the giant's own sword.
Luke 1:42: Blessed are you among women.

translationNotes.note: Not a long battle sword but a short Persian blade worn at the belt. Judith 13:6 uses this word for the weapon hanging on the bedpost, which is why it is within arm's reach of a sleeping man.
A leather provision satchel slung over the shoulder, standard kit for a traveler. It is the same bag her maid carried out of Bethulia holding roasted grain, fig cakes, and bread.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִנָּשִׁים (minashim) - Greek: παρὰ πάσας τὰς γυναῖκας (para pasas tas gynaikas)
translationNotes.note: Hebrew builds a superlative with the word from rather than a separate word for most. Blessed from among women means blessed more than any of them. Judges 5:24 uses the same construction of Jael.
The night watch posted on the wall. Town gates were barred at dusk and left shut until dawn, so anyone returning at night had to call up and be recognized by voice first.

stories.keyTakeaway: Left alone in the tent with Holofernes lying dead drunk, Judith prays, takes his own sword from the bedpost, and cuts off his head with two blows. She and her maid carry it out in the food bag as if going to pray, reach Bethulia, and show the head to the town, where Uzziah blesses her.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 14
summaryBullets: Then Judith said to them, “Listen to me, my friends. Take this head and hang it upon the parapet of your wall. (14:1).

As soon as day breaks and the sun rises on the earth, each of you take up your weapons, and let every able-bodied man go out of the town; set a captain over them, as if you were going down to the plain against the Assyrian outpost; only do not go down. (14:2).

Then they will seize their arms and go into the camp and rouse the officers of the Assyrian army. They will rush into the tent of Holofernes and will not find him. Then panic will come over them, and they will flee before you. (14:3).
Then you and all who live within the borders of Israel will pursue them and cut them down in their tracks. (14:4).
But before you do all this, bring Achior the Ammonite to me so that he may see and recognize the man who despised the house of Israel and sent him to us as if to his death.” (14:5).
So they summoned Achior from the house of Uzziah. When he came and saw the head of Holofernes in the hand of one of the men in the assembly of the people, he fell down on his face in a faint. (14:6).
When they raised him up he threw himself at Judith’s feet and did obeisance to her and said, “Blessed are you in every tent of Judah! In every nation those who hear your name will be alarmed. (14:7).
Now tell me what you have done during these days.” So Judith told him in the presence of the people all that she had done from the day she left until the moment she began speaking to them. (14:8).
When she had finished, the people raised a great shout and made a joyful noise in their town. (14:9).
When Achior saw all that the God of Israel had done, he believed firmly in God. So he was circumcised and joined the house of Israel, remaining so to this day. (14:10).
As soon as it was dawn, they hung the head of Holofernes on the wall. Then they all took their weapons and went out in companies to the mountain passes. (14:11).
When the Assyrians saw them, they sent word to their commanders, who then went to the generals and the captains and to all their other officers. (14:12).

They came to Holofernes’s tent and said to the steward in charge of all his personal affairs, “Wake up our lord, for the slaves have been so bold as to come down against us to give battle, to their utter destruction.” (14:13).
So Bagoas went in and knocked at the entry of the tent, for he supposed that he was sleeping with Judith. (14:14).
But when no one answered, he opened it and went into the bedchamber and found him dead, sprawled over the footstool, with his head missing. (14:15).
He cried out with a loud voice and wept and groaned and shouted and tore his clothes. (14:16).
Then he went to the tent where Judith had stayed, and when he did not find her, he rushed out to the people and shouted, (14:17).
“The slaves have foiled us! One Hebrew woman has brought disgrace on the house of King Nebuchadnezzar. Look, Holofernes is lying on the ground, and his head is missing!” (14:18).
When the leaders of the Assyrian army heard this, they tore their tunics and were greatly dismayed, and their loud cries and shouts rose up throughout the camp. (14:19).
crossRefs: Genesis 17:10-14: Circumcision given as the sign of the covenant.
Exodus 12:48: A resident alien may keep the Passover once circumcised.
1 Samuel 31:9-10: Saul's head cut off and his body fastened to a city wall.
Genesis 37:34: Jacob tears his garments in grief.

translationNotes.note: Deuteronomy 22:8 requires a low guard wall around a flat roof so no one falls off. On a town wall the parapet is the raised edge the defenders stand behind, and anything hung there is visible from the plain below.

translationNotes.term: circumcised and joined the house of Israel
translationNotes.note: Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham in Genesis 17 and the standing requirement for a foreigner who wanted to keep Passover with Israel, Exodus 12:48.
Ripping one's own clothing at the neckline was the standard sign of grief, horror, or outrage. It was done in public on purpose, so that everyone present registered the news at once.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἕως τῆς ἡμέρας ταύτης (heos tes hemeras tautes)
translationNotes.note: A narrator's aside marking something that was still true when the book was written. The same formula runs through Joshua and Judges to explain names, customs, and families still present.

stories.keyTakeaway: Judith has the head hung on the wall and tells the men to march out at dawn as if to attack. Achior faints at the sight, then believes, is circumcised, and joins Israel. Bagoas finds Holofernes dead in his tent and runs out shouting that one Hebrew woman has disgraced the house of Nebuchadnezzar.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 15
summaryBullets: When the men in the tents heard it, they were amazed at what had happened. (15:1).
Overcome with fear and trembling, they did not wait for one another, but with one impulse all rushed out and fled by every path across the plain and through the hill country. (15:2).
Those who had camped in the hills around Bethulia also took to flight. Then the Israelites, everyone who was a soldier, rushed out upon them. (15:3).
Uzziah sent men to Betomasthaim and Choba and Kola and to all the frontiers of Israel to tell what had taken place and to urge all to rush out upon the enemy to destroy them. (15:4).

When the Israelites heard it, with one accord they fell upon the enemy and cut them down as far as Choba. Those in Jerusalem and all the hill country also came, for they were told what had happened in the camp of the enemy. The men in Gilead and in Galilee outflanked them with great slaughter, even beyond Damascus and its borders. (15:5).
The rest of the people of Bethulia fell upon the Assyrian camp and plundered it, acquiring great riches. (15:6).

And the Israelites, when they returned from the slaughter, took possession of what remained. Even the villages and towns in the hill country and in the plain got a great amount of plunder, since there was a vast quantity of it. (15:7).
Then the high priest Joakim and the council of the Israelites who lived in Jerusalem came to witness the good things that the Lord had done for Israel and to see Judith and to wish her well. (15:8).
When they met her, they all blessed her with one accord and said to her, “You are the glory of Jerusalem, you are the great boast of Israel, you are the great pride of our people! (15:9).
You have done all this with your own hand; you have done great good to Israel, and God is well pleased with it. May the Almighty Lord bless you forever!” And all the people said, “Amen.” (15:10).

All the people plundered the camp for thirty days. They gave Judith the tent of Holofernes and all his silver dinnerware, his beds, his bowls, and all his furniture. She took them and loaded her mules and hitched up her carts and piled the things on them. (15:11).

All the women of Israel gathered to see her and blessed her, and some of them performed a dance in her honor. She took ivy-wreathed wands in her hands and distributed them to the women who were with her, (15:12).

and she and those who were with her crowned themselves with olive wreaths. She went before all the people in the dance, leading all the women, while all the men of Israel followed, bearing their arms and wearing garlands and singing hymns. (15:13).
Judith began this thanksgiving before all Israel, and all the people loudly sang this song of praise. (15:14).
crossRefs: Judges 7:21-22: The enemy camp panics in the night and the army flees.
2 Kings 7:15-16: The people plunder an abandoned Aramean camp.
Exodus 15:20-21: Miriam leads the women out with tambourines and dancing.
1 Samuel 18:6-7: Women come out singing and dancing to meet the army.
Numbers 31:25-27: Spoil divided between the fighters and the community.

translationNotes.note: A staff wound with ivy, carried in Greek festival processions. The Greek text of 15:12 describes Israel's victory dance using an object its Greek-speaking readers would picture at once.
A circlet of leaves worn on the head by victors and celebrants. Wreaths were made on the spot and worn for the day, which is a different thing from a metal crown.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֹּהֵן גָּדוֹל (kohen gadol) - Greek: ἀρχιερεύς (archiereus)
translationNotes.note: The chief priest of the Jerusalem temple, who also presided over the council of elders. In the Persian and Greek periods he was the ranking Jewish authority in civil matters as well as worship.
Silver plate, bowls, and serving vessels. Wealth traveled as metalwork and livestock rather than coin on this scale, so a general's table service was portable capital.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Assyrians panic and scatter, and Israel pursues them as far as Choba while men of Gilead and Galilee cut them down beyond Damascus. Bethulia plunders the camp for thirty days. Joakim and the council come from Jerusalem to bless Judith, and the women crown themselves and dance behind her.

stories.title: ⚔️ Judith 16
summaryBullets: And Judith said, “Begin a song to my God with tambourines; sing to my Lord with cymbals. Raise to him a new psalm; exalt him and call upon his name. (16:1).
For the Lord is a God who crushes wars; he sets up his camp among his people; he delivered me from the hands of my pursuers. (16:2).
The Assyrian came down from the mountains of the north; he came with myriads of his warriors; their numbers blocked up the wadis, and their cavalry covered the hills. (16:3).
He boasted that he would burn up my territory and kill my young men with the sword and dash my infants to the ground and seize my children as plunder and take my virgins as spoil. (16:4).
“But the Lord Almighty has foiled them by the hand of a woman. (16:5).

For their mighty one did not fall by the hands of the young men, nor did the sons of the Titans strike him down, nor did tall giants set upon him, but Judith daughter of Merari with the beauty of her countenance undid him. (16:6).
“For she put away her widow’s clothing to exalt the oppressed in Israel. She anointed her face with perfume; (16:7).
she fastened her hair with a tiara and put on a linen gown to beguile him. (16:8).
Her sandal ravished his eyes, her beauty captivated his mind, and the sword severed his neck! (16:9).
The Persians trembled at her boldness; the Medes were daunted at her daring. (16:10).
“Then my oppressed people shouted; my weak people cried out, and the enemy trembled; they lifted up their voices, and the enemy were turned back. (16:11).
Sons of female slaves pierced them through and wounded them like the children of fugitives; they perished before the army of my Lord. (16:12).
