“I will sing to my God a new song: O Lord, you are great and glorious, wonderful in strength, invincible. (16:13).
Let all your creatures serve you, for you spoke, and they were made. You sent forth your spirit, and it formed them; there is none that can resist your voice. (16:14).
For the mountains shall be shaken to their foundations with the waters; before your glance the rocks shall melt like wax. But to those who fear you you show mercy. (16:15).
For every sacrifice as a fragrant offering is a small thing, and the fat of all whole burnt offerings to you is a very little thing, but whoever fears the Lord is great forever. (16:16).

“Woe to the nations that rise up against my people! The Lord Almighty will take vengeance on them in the day of judgment; he will send fire and worms into their flesh; they shall weep in pain forever.” (16:17).
When they arrived at Jerusalem, they worshiped God. As soon as the people were purified, they offered their burnt offerings, their freewill offerings, and their gifts. (16:18).
Judith also dedicated to God all the possessions of Holofernes that the people had given her, and the canopy that she had taken for herself from his bedchamber she gave as a votive offering. (16:19).
For three months the people continued feasting in Jerusalem before the sanctuary, and Judith remained with them. (16:20).
After this they all returned home to their own inheritances. Judith went to Bethulia and remained on her estate. For the rest of her life she was honored throughout the whole country. (16:21).
Many desired to marry her, but she gave herself to no man all the days of her life after her husband Manasseh died and was gathered to his people. (16:22).

She became more and more famous and grew old in her husband’s house, reaching the age of one hundred five. She set her maid free. She died in Bethulia, and they buried her in the cave of her husband Manasseh, (16:23).
and the house of Israel mourned her for seven days. Before she died she distributed her property to all those who were next of kin to her husband Manasseh and to her own nearest kindred. (16:24).
No one ever again spread terror among the Israelites during the lifetime of Judith or for a long time after her death. (16:25).
crossRefs: Exodus 15:1-21: The song sung after the enemy is destroyed at the sea.
Judges 5:1-31: Deborah and Barak sing of the battle and its outcome.
1 Samuel 2:1-10: Hannah sings that the Lord brings low and lifts up.
Isaiah 66:24: Fire and worm as the end of those who rebelled.
Genesis 50:10: Seven days of mourning kept for the dead.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁיר חָדָשׁ (shir chadash) - Greek: ψαλμὸς καινός (psalmos kainos)
translationNotes.note: A fixed phrase for a song composed for a fresh act of deliverance, as in Psalm 96:1 and Psalm 98:1. It means newly written for this occasion, not a new style of music.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רְפָאִים (Rephaim) - Greek: υἱοὶ τιτάνων (huioi titanon)
translationNotes.note: The Greek translators used Titans, the giant race of Greek myth, to render the Hebrew Rephaim. The Greek of 2 Samuel 5:18 and 5:22 calls the Valley of Rephaim the valley of the Titans.
An object vowed to God and handed over to the sanctuary permanently, displayed there rather than burned. Luke 21:5 uses the same Greek word for the gifts that decorated the temple.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁבְעָה (shivah) - Greek: ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας (hepta hemeras)
translationNotes.note: A set seven-day mourning period, kept for Jacob in Genesis 50:10 and for Saul in 1 Samuel 31:13. Judith receives it from the whole house of Israel rather than her household alone.

stories.keyTakeaway: Judith leads a thanksgiving song telling how the Lord crushed the Assyrian by the hand of a woman. At Jerusalem she dedicates Holofernes' goods and his canopy as a votive offering. She frees her maid, never remarries, dies at one hundred five, and Israel mourns her seven days.

intro:
Judith does not name its author, and the early church named none for it. Clement of Rome cites the book in his Letter to the Corinthians 55 (c. AD 96), recalling that Judith asked the elders for leave to go out into the camp of the strangers and that the Lord delivered Holofernes into the hand of a woman, which puts it in use at Rome in the first century AD. No Hebrew or Aramaic copy has survived from antiquity, and none was found at Qumran. Jerome states in his preface to Judith that he translated from an Aramaic copy in a single night's work, and that he took the job on because the Council of Nicaea was reckoned to have counted Judith among the sacred Scriptures. His Latin, made about AD 407, runs shorter than the Greek.

The setting is a campaign against the western nations. The book dates itself to the twelfth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, who ruled over the Assyrians in the great city of Nineveh (1:1), when Arphaxad ruled the Medes at Ecbatana and had walled it with hewn stone (1:2-4). The west refuses his summons to war, so he swears revenge, defeats and kills Arphaxad in the mountains of Ragau in his seventeenth year (1:11-15), and in his eighteenth year sends Holofernes, chief general of the army and second only to himself, west with a hundred and twenty thousand foot and twelve thousand mounted archers (2:4-5; 2:15). The line of march is given stage by stage: out of Nineveh to the plain of Bectileth below Upper Cilicia, then through Put and Lud, Mesopotamia, Cilicia, the Midianites, and the plain of Damascus at wheat harvest, down to the coast from Sidon and Tyre to Ascalon (2:21-28). The coastal cities surrender; Holofernes garrisons them and pulls down their shrines so that every nation will call on Nebuchadnezzar as god (3:6-8), then camps between Geba and Scythopolis near Dothan, facing the ridge of Judea (3:9-10).

In Judea the people have only lately come back from exile, and the altar and the sacred vessels have just been reconsecrated after their profanation (4:3). The high priest Joakim, with the council of the whole people at Jerusalem, orders Bethulia and Betomesthaim, facing Esdraelon near Dothan, to hold the mountain passes, the approach being wide enough for only two men abreast (4:6-8). Holofernes brings a hundred and seventy thousand foot and twelve thousand horse against Bethulia and, on Edomite and Moabite advice, seizes the spring below the mountain rather than force the pass, so that after thirty-four days the cisterns run dry (7:2; 7:8-20). Achior the Ammonite leader, who told him this people cannot be beaten unless they sin against their God, has been bound and left below the town (5:5-21; 6:10-13), and Bagoas, a eunuch, keeps Holofernes' household (12:11). Judith is a widow of Bethulia, daughter of Merari, her line traced back sixteen generations to Israel (8:1) and her prayer claiming Simeon for an ancestor (9:2); her husband Manasseh had died of sunstroke in the barley harvest (8:2-3). She dies at Bethulia at one hundred five (16:23).

Which ruler and which campaign the book refers to is an open question, since Scripture gives no second account of this war. Both officers' names are attested in the Persian period. Diodorus Siculus names a Holophernes, son of Ariamnes and brother of Ariarathes of Cappadocia, who fought for Artaxerxes III Ochus (reigned 359-338 BC) in the Persian reconquest of Egypt (Library of History 31.19.2-3), and names a eunuch Bagoas as that king's most trusted man and a commander of the same campaign (16.47). Judith stands among the historical books in the Greek codices beside Tobit and Esther, and after Tobit in the Vulgate. The Council of Hippo (AD 393) listed Judith among the canonical books and the Councils of Carthage (AD 397 and 419) repeated that list; the Council of Trent (session 4, AD 1546) affirmed it, and the Synod of Jerusalem under Patriarch Dositheus (AD 1672) named it a genuine part of Scripture for the Eastern Orthodox. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles (AD 1571) places Judith among the books the Church of England reads for example of life but not to establish doctrine. The Hebrew name behind the title is Yehudit (יְהוּדִית), the feminine of Yehudi, meaning "Jewess" or "woman of Judah"; the Greek form is Ioudith (Ἰουδίθ). Jewish practice keeps the account at Hanukkah: Moses Isserles, the Rema (AD 1520-1572), records in his gloss to the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chayim 670:2) the custom of eating cheese at the feast in memory of Judith.
